claims.text: The as-cast HfNbTaTiZr alloy has a heterogeneous microstructure.
The as-cast alloy contains pronounced local short-range chemical order.
The as-cast alloy contains inherent lattice distortions and possible compositional fluctuations.
A homogenization anneal above 1000 °C can reduce or otherwise modify local short-range order by equilibrating chemical fluctuations.
Thermal-expansion mismatch at elevated temperature biases chemical-ordering kinetics and produces pronounced short-range order.
Atomic-size differences produce lattice distortions or mismatch in HfNbTaTiZr.
Short-range order generates internal stress fields.
The internal stress fields generated by short-range order pin dislocations during deformation.
Short-range order modulates phase stability.
The proposed short-range-order mechanism affects tensile creep at 1250 °C.
The proposed short-range-order mechanism affects hardening during cold rolling.
The proposed short-range-order mechanism affects elastic-modulus and thermal-expansion responses.
Relative to the as-cast baseline, a homogenized sample with reduced short-range order will have fewer internal stress fields.
A homogenized sample with reduced short-range order will have a lower creep rate at 1250 °C.
The lower predicted creep rate is caused by having fewer internal stress fields that hinder dislocation motion.
A homogenized sample with reduced short-range order will show a smaller microhardness increase after cold rolling.
A homogenized sample with reduced short-range order will exhibit smoother and more linear elastic-modulus and thermal-expansion responses from 293 to 1100 K.
Thermal-expansion mismatch is particularly significant above 1000 °C.
Heterogeneous short-range order in the untreated alloy produces higher internal stress fields and increased creep rates.
Heterogeneous short-range order in the untreated alloy produces stronger cold-work hardening and anomalous thermoelastic behavior.

contradictions.description: The mechanism says SRO-generated internal stress fields pin dislocations, but the predicted outcome says reducing those pinning fields lowers creep rate. Removing obstacles to dislocation motion would ordinarily imply greater mobility, so the stated direction of the creep prediction conflicts with the proposed mechanism.

The mechanism characterizes internal stress fields as dislocation-pinning obstacles, whereas the baseline says higher internal stress fields manifest as increased creep rates. No additional mechanism is supplied to reconcile stronger pinning with faster creep.
